title: The Fruits of Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Umbrella Man, a book of appreciations by Sojun Mel Weitsman's Dharma heirs for his 80th birthday, sorting the quotations under themes such as steadiness, humility, ordinariness, and deep listening. After an opening story about Zazen loosening a tense, overworked afternoon before vacation, Nomon retells the koan of the teacher polishing a roof tile to make a mirror. One quoted student asks Mel when to hit the clackers and gets the answer "Hit them when it feels right." Another student describes Mel nodding off during dokusan until the student's voice turned fresh. Nomon then notes what the book leaves out, since nobody praises Mel for being right or brilliant, and closes with an offer to officiate anyone's funeral and a request that sangha members say what should happen to their belongings.

verbatim.text: Today, in the last couple of days, I've been working a little bit too hard because we're going on vacation tomorrow. But anyway, I was getting really caught, and especially this afternoon, I was quite caught by the desire to produce and create and prove myself and all these things.

Getting tense in the shoulders and sort of feeling that sort of psychic sort of turtle feeling that one feels when one's sort of trying too hard. I was doing good work, actually, with this sort of extra cost and extra overhead. And I was just realizing, standing there, I never would have come to Zazen if I didn't feel obligated to come. I would have tried to get a little more work done and started packing for the trip and run around a lot. And so I was really feeling grateful and sort of amazed, sort of amazed anew at the way something this simple could be so effective at that kind of psychic unbending, that kind of healing from clinging. When I first sat down for Zazen, I felt naturally tense in the body and resistant to Zazen. And so I was thinking, you know, we should really do some stretching first. What a stupid system we have. We agree to obligate each other and obligate ourselves during practice period. But really we need that all the time. Tempered with realism of what we can do and what we have time for, we need to feel probably some sense of obligation. Because when we need practice most is when we don't want to come. It's when we really don't want to come. So we need that decision to not be in that usual category. So anyway, that's just a little prologue. So I'll be gone in the next two weeks.

So I thought I would give the same talk, more or less, that I gave at our one day sesshin a week and a half ago.

Which went really well. So a few of us have heard this talk before and most of us haven't. It was a very beautiful sesshin. Hopefully we'll get to do that again. So in this talk I want to look at the example of somebody else. Somebody who's practiced for a long time.

In this case a Zen teacher has practiced for more than 40 years. Because this teacher, his name is Sojun Mel Weitsman, Sojun Mel Weitsman. He ended up being an important sort of, not last exactly, but sort of finishing teacher for quite a few American Zen teachers. About 20. Where they started their training with other people. Steadiness, devotion, and endurance. It seems to me that the main characteristic of Suzuki Roshi's teaching and of Soto Zen is faith and steadiness and endurance to keep going with the practice, no matter what. As Dogen taught so profoundly, the practice is enlightenment. There is no enlightenment outside of practice. In the early days, and I know it's the same now, it was clear without anyone needing to say so that this was the value most encouraged by Mel. There was sitting every morning at 5 a.m.

And Mel was there every day, always on time. Whether there was one person or two or three joining him, and there was seldom more than three or four in the early days, he would always be there, sitting in his place at the head of the stairs. So that when you walked up the stairs, you would see him first. Just there, always there, motionless and quiet. Generous and steadfast, steadfast. And he was steadfast.

Now that I look back at those years when he was there in the hinterlands and the Big Zen thing was happening in San Francisco, and Mel was quietly running his smaller center in Berkeley, he just steadfastly practiced, taught, and followed his way. Followed Suzuki Roshi's way. Just a tremendous steadfast quality and not fancy. Mel is not a very fancy kind of person. No frills.

Very different from the flavor of the way Richard Baker taught. Humble. Associated with all this is tremendous humility. Steve Stuckey, Paul Haller and I did Dharma transmission with Mel in 1993. Each of us had to do a series of ceremonies. After the final Dharma talk, we went to Suzuki Roshi's ashes site up on the hog back, so where Suzuki Roshi's ashes are buried. Thanks.

Some of them. We offered incense and bowed, and Mel was standing in front of Suzuki Roshi, and the three of us were a little further back. Thanks. Mel looked at us and said, you know, this is a very pregnant moment, right? So the Dharma transmission ceremony takes a week, and it's like sort of continuous effort,

and for some reason, the tradition is the most important parts of the ceremony are done in the middle of the night, like literally, like one, two, eight in the morning. So you're really tired, I would think, and you know, you've been through this huge thing, and now you're at the memorial site of Suzuki Roshi, so you can imagine that feeling. We stood there, and Mel looked at us and said, I'm not so good, but you are good, and went on to say that passing on the Dharma to us was a good thing,

and that we would manifest it in a good way, good things would happen. This statement, I'm not so good, but you are good, is one of the most important things that anyone has ever said to me, not because it makes me good, but because the quality of humility is so authentic. When I teach and practice now, I hope I convey that spirit,

letting go of results. The evolution of my sense of zazen is a lot about polishing a tile, challenging the whole idea that you're going to get somewhere, or get something out of it. Now I'm not as focused on getting something, or being in some particular way. In zazen, or in general, I'm not as focused on that as I used to be.

I realize, wherever I am, it's not going to be so good. It's not going to be the way I want it, so I might as well get used to it. Dogen said, those who have great realization of delusion are Buddha. Those who have great realization of delusion are Buddha. You know there's no place to go. The place where you get to be a Buddha, so to speak, is in delusion, and there's plenty to go around.

And you get up where you fall down. I like to talk about that too. You get up where you fall down. Where else would you get up? You don't get up somewhere else. It's where you fall down that you establish your practice. That's what Mel manifested when he talked to me during our training. Supportive and open and friendly and helpful,

just assisting me in getting up where I fell down. And the first line of that, the evolution of my sense of zazen is a lot about polishing. A tile is a koan reference. Let me mention that story to you. You've probably heard this story. It's from China. So there's a student who's a really determined meditation student.

It really feels obligated, overly obligated. Always sitting zazen. It comes to all the regular periods, but also during the breaks and treats every day like sesshin and is always, always practicing. Constantly sitting zazen. And then one day the teacher comes along and maybe he was sitting on the outside of the zendo.

There's usually a porch on the outside. So maybe he's sitting on this porch on the outside called the angawa in Japanese. Because the teacher picked up a roof tile, so they must have been working on the roof, those ceramic tiles. So the teacher picks up a roof tile and gets out his handkerchief

and starts rubbing the tile with it, standing like right in the face of the student sitting zazen so assiduously, just rubbing this roof tile. And finally the student gets exasperated and says, well, why are you polishing the tile like that? And the teacher says, I'm making a mirror. I'm making a mirror out of this tile.

And the student says, you can't polish a tile into a mirror. That's not possible. And the teacher says something like, well, you can't make a Buddha by sitting zazen like that. It's the same thing. So that's a famous story that's about the student is Zhao Zhou,

who goes on to be also a famous Chinese master later, and the teacher is his teacher Nan Chuang. So that's a good story for us. We need to be obligated, but we don't need to try to polish a tile into a mirror. The next quality. Just being upright. Just being upright.

Once I was studying my tendency to be regarded as a good guy by everyone. Do you know that tendency? I asked Mel, I know the true Dharma goes beyond the duality of good and bad, but isn't it valid to choose the good? After a brief pause,

Mel looked me in the eye and said, our practice is being upright. Just being upright. Connecting to the feeling of practice. Not just the idea of the feeling of practice. When Mel was the abbot, he at one point went over to San Francisco's Ange Center to help them as the abbot.

When Mel was the abbot and I was the eno, managing the zendo, I wanted to clarify one of the details of qing hing. So I asked Mel, okay, when do we hit the clackers? He looked at me with conviction and said, hit them when it feels right. That was his notion of precision.

Not just a notion of precision, but an invitation to attend to precision, the precision of being in tune with the whole activity. Being in tune with the whole activity. That story always makes me think of these detailed scripts we have. We don't have everything scripted

and we always want to have more things scripted. We have some things quite well scripted. Which I think is good. It makes it more possible for people to jump in and try these things. Don did a lovely job with about two minutes training hitting the han because we have it all scripted. But the thing is,

it's not really about following the script. Eventually you need to feel it in your body. Unfortunately the scripts also have mistakes in them. Which I keep not getting around to fixing. Maybe on purpose. It's good to have flawed scripts. Connecting to the feeling of practice. Working with difficulties.

Working with difficulties. When significant difficulties arose at Berkeley's end center, how they were handled was admirable. In a direct way, his senior students were always saying, or were saying, Hey Mel, what are you doing?

Without defensiveness, he'd respond, Oh, you're right. But he didn't say, Okay well, then you can't be my student. And they didn't say, Well you can't be our teacher. Mel had trained them and worked with them in a way

that whatever the issue, their relationship could be sustained. And they worked it through. Good training for us. Which is definitely our hope here. We can have that feeling of understanding and sense of safety. It's like Jeff bringing us the full value contract.

Same idea. Ordinariness. Ordinariness. For me, Sojun Roshi's genius is in his ordinariness. Once at a big hospice fundraising dinner at Green's Restaurant in San Francisco, a very fancy restaurant everyone would be dressed up. Ram Dass was the guest speaker.

I knew that Sojun would be making a speech right after him. Ram Dass was a famous spiritual teacher. I began to wonder what Sojun would do. How would he express himself to all these potential donors and people from the wider community? When his turn came, Sojun got up and spoke to the crowd,

just like he always spoke. The same old Sojun. The same one I know in the Zendo, in the Dooksan room, and at Zen Center staff meetings. It's hard to put into words how much Sojun's lack of desire to make a big impression on others impressed me.

It's easy to say, just accept who you are. Or as Suzuki Roshi said, when you are completely you, Zen is Zen. But it is rare to have a living model of this. I am very grateful to Sojun for his embodiment of this teaching. From this first encounter,

I was inspired by what I took to be Mel's ordinariness. He wasn't trying to impress anybody or stand out in any way. He seemed like a very ordinary, accessible person. And yet, in that ordinariness was something that meant a lot to me. It seemed to me that he was the first person I'd met

who was settled and at peace with himself. I saw in Mel a form of everyday, straightforward Zen practice that didn't make Zen into something esoteric or mysterious, appreciating disagreement. Mel wanted to know how I understood my relationship to him.

I told him I trusted him implicitly, but I didn't know if I agreed completely with his Dharma understanding. To my amazement, he stopped. They were walking along. He stopped. Mel turned to me and said in a very direct, welcoming way something like,

Great! Where we disagree is where we can meet. I believe he also brought his hands together to emphasize that meeting, being yourself. More than anyone else, I see Suzuki Roshi in Mel's face. I myself tried for several years

to be Suzuki Roshi. It's okay that you've died, I thought. You can have my life. But I ended up abandoning myself when I tried to practice that way. But Mel is just Mel. And there's Suzuki Roshi, deep listening.

After my Dharma transmission, I said to Sojun, Remember, I'm not going to start a Zen group. That's not what I do. He didn't say anything. A few years later, I started a Zen group. And it was thriving.

I was again talking with Sojun. And I reminded him with a little embarrassment of my earlier comment. I guess you must have known something back then that I didn't, I said. He replied, Oh, I don't listen to what people say. Right.

What he meant was, I don't listen to what people say. I listen to what people say. And I've tried to do that in my own work as a priest. Another one about listening. I felt deeply known, seen, and accepted by Mel.

He was interested. He listened. I was totally neurotic at the time and had so many problems. Yet his mind was so wide that whatever yammering was happening in my mind would just float away into the ether as I talked. After five minutes of talking to him,
my gigantic problems, of which I had many, floated away in his big mind. There was nothing else to say, so we'd just sit there, quiet and content. He never answered. He never solved anything.

I couldn't have articulated this at the time, but I was going there to be with his mind. I would talk for five or ten minutes and then we'd be quiet and I'd sit in his spaciousness. Little by little, learning, that's the best thing we have to offer other people
from our practice, that sense of space. Being with others or teaching with others. In relationship with people who came to study the Dharma with me, I can see now how deeply I've been shaped
by Sojun Roshi's way. Aum, grow up, Svaha. That's this teacher's mantra. Aum, grow up, Svaha. Take seriously your life as it is. Make it a Buddha field of generosity and mutuality. Sit Zazen.

Be honest with yourself and others. Don't fall for fancy ideas about practice. Keep at it. As a teacher, you can rely on me to show up and share my understanding, but not to tell you what to do. It is up to you to realize the way.

Find joy in the feel of your feet on the floor. Live in your world. This is some of what I received from Mel. It is my life's work to live out all I have been given. Another one about being straightforward. Being straightforward.
Sojun values and embodies directness. He cuts through delusion. No hesitation. My experience is that this comes directly from Zazen. He is quite willing to tell me my stuff, to show me my shadow.

Usually he is right. It is sometimes painful to hear, but helpful. Once I had been harboring ill will towards a dear friend and could not let it go. I found I kept trying to convince her that she was wrong about an exchange
and that it had hurt me deeply. Finally, I went to Sojun and told him about my difficulty in letting the matter drop. Once, can't you just say ouch and move on? And as is my practice
with him, I said yes and left. She didn't know how she was going to do that, but she said yes. Then I practiced with it. I found that I had neither voiced nor let myself experience the ouch.
And so I did. First experiencing it myself and then meeting with my friend about it. She apologized. We both dropped it and moved on, working honestly with faults. I have seen Sojun Roshi

when he was accused of crossing boundaries. This happened with gay students at Tassajara Monastery and with women students at Berkeley at different times. What impressed me was how open Sojun was with the students who confronted him.
Somehow he managed to demonstrate humility and yet not be servile. He always maintained his dignity and authority. About a year ago in Shosan, which is like a formal question and answer ceremony,
somebody asked him what his greatest difficulty as a teacher was. Without hesitation he said, I tend to fall in love with my female students. I work with this by trying to think of them as sisters.

I was deeply moved by his honesty. Boredom is okay. Or maybe boredom is good. Over the years, Mel's presentation of the Dharma has often put me to sleep. I aspire to this. Too much trying to be interesting.
It puts me to sleep until the unique quality of his teaching begins to permeate my bones. And then I wake up, deeply nourished. He would talk about the virtues of ordinary conventional life

and he would go through the teachings word by word, reading them again and again. When Mel and I would meet for Dokusan, private interview, every so often, I began to notice that whenever I started going on and on about my problems, he would fall asleep.

Often right in the middle of presenting an important emotional reaction. It was something that had happened. I would gradually notice him nodding. Sometimes he would open his eyes very wide to try to stay with me. But when my voice became authentic
and fresh, he would completely wake up. This boring approach taught me an important lesson about how to meet Dharma and life. When a situation or a person presents itself in an unresolved,
undeveloped way, one can meet it with a matter of fact self-nourishing patience. Mel's Dharma is to offer a few words, but then stay until awakening occurs. I like that phrase

that the person wrote. One can meet it with a matter of fact self-nourishing patience. For some reason I really find this last quote really helpful, working with my desire to be exciting or something.
I think we all have this impulse to be clever, to be interesting, to give good advice, to be right, but to let ourselves be boring and ordinary just to listen and attend to the moment.
Giving space is a good teaching for us, good for me. I just want to read you my somewhat arbitrary list of qualities again I pulled out of this book. Let's talk for a minute about what's not there.
Steadyness, devotion, and endurance, generosity, being steadfast, humble, letting go of results, being upright, connecting to the feeling, working with difficulties,
being ordinary, and being being ordinary, being yourself, appreciating disagreement, and not trying to be someone else, deep listening,
teaching others, being straightforward, working honestly with faults, and boredom is okay. I'm going to change that for the future to boredom is good. And then we can think about

what we project on ourselves, what we desire from ourselves, and what we desire and project upon our teachers. Nobody talked about how Mel was always right about them. One person said that Mel would be incisive
about her shadow side. Other people said they didn't agree with Mel or didn't get any advice from Mel. The consensus was not anything about being right or being smart, or brilliant, or insightful.
Instead they talked about steadiness, devotion to practice, nothing flashy or impressive, being ordinary, settling in to our life, accepting the moment that arises
fully, without embellishment or resistance, and some, through some strange chain of circumstances, we have the opportunity to do the exact same practice
that Sojun Roshi, whom I think probably no one but me here has actually even met, but that's okay, to join him in steady practice of zazen and extending that feeling out into our life,

returning regularly to this so supportive container, like I was appreciating tonight, and not diffusing our energy any more than our karma mandates. It's not getting any more confused than we have to.
And if we do have hard times, which we will, to have in our bodies some feeling cultivated quietly over a long time that we can touch and turn to, to help us remember, and to have some faith

that just by being ordinary and fully being ourselves, we can be so helpful to others, that rather than trying harder to be just the right kind of person, figuring out what we need to do, there's a way we can slip under that
impulse and find the most helpful person. And the other way this is important, I think, we're reminded by the fact that this is Sojun's 80th birthday, so who knows how much longer he'll live.

And then also, before Zaza and I went down to the office and I looked in my box, and there was a mailer from a fellow offering discount funeral and cremation services. I don't know about discount. Reasonable.

It says a reasonable. Discount sounds pejorative. I don't know what he's doing. We're reminded that this essential fact in the background always that we are so good at forgetting about our own mortality.

A way to look at practice is preparation for that last hour of our life. And we know that there will be a last hour. And in that last hour, can we give our life away? Can we give teachings and healing to ourselves and our loved ones, whether they're with us or far away?

And a practical point is if you'd like me to do your funeral, you should let me know. We're one of the things that a community should know about each other. We don't have any legal power. It'll be your family that steps in, whoever they are.

I'm sure there are wills and documents one is supposed to have that probably none of us have gotten around to. Okay, John can tell us how to do it. Because we're going to leave behind a few hundred pounds of stuff. So it's helpful to let everyone know what you want done with it.
